item.content:encoded:
THE ELECTION RESULTS REINFORCE A FAMILIAR POLITICAL LESSON: ECONOMIC CONDITIONS AND HOUSEHOLD PURCHASING POWER REMAIN CENTRAL TO VOTER SENTIMENT. The breadth of Republican losses suggests meaningful dissatisfaction with the direction of the administration, particularly around issues affecting households and everyday economic well-being. Concerns about the cost of living, tariffs, and the economic consequences of the Iran conflict have weighed on voters. Accountability was another important consideration…the AP voter survey found more than half of voters considered government corruption crucial to their congressional vote, slightly more than the share citing the cost of living. The broader takeaway is that affordability and confidence in government remain closely intertwined, with voters looking for policies that deliver tangible improvements in their everyday lives. The coalition that returned Trump to office also proved more conditional than claims of a durable political realignment suggested…56% of men under 30 backed him in 2024, yet 59% supported Democratic House candidates this time. The Democratic margin among Hispanic women also widened to 36 percentage points from 21 points in 2024. Presidential and midterm elections draw different electorates, but the primary lesson is that support must be continually earned. Democrats should therefore recognise this as more a moment than a mandate…52% of midterm voters still viewed their party unfavourably. Rejection of the current administration gives them an opportunity to rebuild trust but treating it as unconditional approval of their entire ideological programme would risk repeating the GOP’s mistake. In that respect, the larger House majority reduces Hakeem Jeffries’ dependence on the progressive left, giving leadership more room to govern from the centre. My sense is that this could also strengthen the prospects of a more moderate presidential nominee in 2028. Moreover, that freedom should be used to demonstrate competence and restore credible oversight…making impeachment the centrepiece of the next two years would be a mistake. Another all-consuming confrontation with little prospect of removal would risk distracting from the practical concerns that delivered this majority. Evidence-led investigations into alleged self-dealing and conflicts of interest are a more useful exercise of accountability, alongside a practical governing agenda. Republicans, meanwhile, face the task of rebuilding with a congressional party still heavily identified with Trump. One central choice is whether to double down on a Vance-led version of America First or move towards a more traditional Reagan-style Republicanism centred on markets, fiscal discipline, and alliances. Either route requires an honest assessment of why voters withdrew their support…changing the messenger achieves little without a convincing response to voter concerns. Ultimately, the significance of these elections transcends party affiliation. America’s constitutional framework and system of checks and balances have demonstrated their resilience…the public has retained the power to hold its leaders accountable and change the direction of government. In my mind, that capacity for correction is a powerful affirmation of American democracy and an enduring source of strength for the country. It should reinforce confidence in the resilience of its institutions over the long term, whilst reminding both parties that public trust must be continually earned. Political power remains conditional on listening to the American people and serving them.

 

THE POLITICS OF AI ARE FORCING A REASSESSMENT OF THE BUILDOUT. I have been writing about this since May, when I highlighted the uncomfortable parallel with globalisation…diffuse, long-term benefits offer limited political protection when communities believe they are bearing immediate costs through higher electricity bills, pressure on local resources and the prospect of job displacement. The midterms have given those concerns greater political weight…Democratic control of Congress allows for closer scrutiny, but the more immediate constraints come through states such as Texas, where permitting and grid connections determine the pace and scale of data centre construction. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s commitment to maintain a moratorium until stronger protections are legislated raises the risk of prolonged delays. The market has understandably focused on the implications for AI capex, but I would be wary of assuming Democrats will stop construction altogether. Pennsylvania’s Shapiro administration already offers greater permitting speed and certainty to projects meeting standards on electricity affordability and community benefits. There is a potential bargain here…developers shoulder more of the costs they impose, and communities gain a clearer interest in allowing projects to proceed. My base case is longer delays, tougher conditions and selective resumption…with some projects relocated or abandoned along the way.

 

FOR INVESTORS, THIS SHARPENS THE DISTINCTION between compute that is already operating and capacity that still needs to be permitted, financed, and connected. Assuming demand for compute continues to exceed available supply, restricting incremental capacity should support utilisation and the scarcity value of the installed base. This reinforces my relative preference for hyperscalers with operational compute, secure power access, financial flexibility, and several routes to monetisation. There was evidence of this dynamic in the market this week, with hyperscalers outperforming semis. For projects still awaiting delivery, restrictions can push revenues further into the future whilst financing and development costs continue to accumulate…raising the return investors should demand for funding the buildout. Frank Flight’s Wednesday note captured the rotation towards a “peak AI capex” theme…slower delivery of powered buildings can leave component production running ahead of installation, exposing hardware suppliers to order deferrals and excess inventories even whilst usable compute remains scarce. In my view, this raises the premium on capacity that can earn a return today…and the hurdle for capital committed to its future delivery.

 

STEPPING BACK, I THINK THE POLITICAL AND MARKET IMPLICATIONS OF THESE ELECTIONS are connected by a common principle…economic progress ultimately depends on retaining the consent of those expected to bear its costs. The same electorate that punished an administration for neglecting household affordability is now imposing constraints on an investment cycle whose aggregate economic promise has often obscured its more immediate local consequences. I remain constructive on the long-term demand for AI, but increasingly selective about where the economic rents from that demand will accrue. Slower capacity additions may ultimately reinforce the pricing power of those already operating scarce compute, even as they undermine the economics of suppliers dependent on an uninterrupted construction boom. There is a broader lesson here for both policymakers and investors…technological progress does not occur in a political vacuum, and the distribution of its costs and benefits can be as consequential as their aggregate magnitude. The AI investment cycle is unlikely to end here, but its next phase may be shaped as much by political consent and the scarcity of usable capacity as by the extraordinary technological possibilities that set it in motion.

item.title: Houston, Do We Have A Problem?
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: The midterm election results have important implications for the US macro outlook, with a more challenging environment for the AI investment cycle, a potentially accelerated resolution to the Iran conflict and a political realignment towards the centre ahead of 2028 . item.content:encoded:
The midterm election results have important implications for the US macro outlook, with a more challenging environment for the AI investment cycle, a potentially accelerated resolution to the Iran conflict and a political realignment towards the centre ahead of 2028. The electoral backlash against data-centre development introduces new constraints on the pace of AI infrastructure deployment, although the geographical mobility of capital should limit the ultimate impact on aggregate investment. The more immediate consequences are likely to be slower construction, greater execution risk and a redistribution of returns along the AI supply chain, favouring businesses with operational and energized compute over hardware suppliers exposed to deployment delays. For index level risk assets, these headwinds may be offset if the Iran war reaches a quicker diplomatic settlement than previously expected. The scale of the Republican defeat may create some urgency in Washington to negotiate which could align with Tehran’s apparent incentive to monetise its remaining leverage. Meanwhile, the breadth of the swing against Republicans, alongside the relative outperformance of centrist Democrats, suggests a political recalibration towards the centre as both parties look ahead to 2028. We therefore see competing forces for equities, likely to manifest in a “Peak Capex” rotation, but a more consistent directional impulse for rates, with slower near-term investment, a marginal reduction in near term financing demand and the prospect of lower energy prices all favouring lower yields.

The election suggests the data-centre buildout may face a tougher regulatory and permitting environment. 56% of voters described AI and data centres as a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote and voters opposed data centre development in at least 39 of the 45 local ballot initiatives on the issue. The potential exposure is substantial, with around 45 GW across 350 projects in Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Georgia at risk between 2026–30, including 24 GW in Texas alone, a state accounting for a substantial share of planned/marginal US capacity by 2030. Viewed through the lens of general equilibrium, however, the impact on aggregate investment is likely to be considerably smaller, as restrictions in one jurisdiction create incentives for capital and construction to migrate elsewhere eventually. Provided demand for compute remains strong, restrictions in one jurisdiction should encourage investment to migrate towards others willing and able to accommodate it, with the scarcity of available capacity sustaining the incentive to build. Securing alternative sites, power and approvals takes time, so this adjustment could still materially delay deployment and raise costs. We would therefore expect some moderation in the near-term growth and inflation impulse from construction and associated resource demand, alongside a smaller impact on cumulative investment and financing requirements.

The rotational consequences of the election we think diverge sharply along the supply chain, with markets increasingly likely to chase a “peak AI capex” theme, rotating out of memory, neoclouds and energy, and into staples, healthcare, banks, housing, retail and, in line with our Tokenomics 2.0 view: the hyperscalers themselves. The underlying intuition is that a slower buildout could be relatively favourable for those doing the spending, and potentially less so for those receiving it. For the hardware “picks and shovels”, slower delivery of powered buildings raises the risk that component production runs ahead of installation, leaving suppliers exposed to order deferrals and excess inventories even while usable compute remains scarce; this vulnerability is likely most pronounced in memory, optical and other semiconductor components.

For cloud businesses already selling energised compute, or bringing fully permitted capacity with secured power online shortly, delayed competition should instead support utilisation, pricing power and prospective margins, while reducing the risk of an eventual capacity glut. For the hyperscalers themselves, some moderation in the pace of capital expenditure should also provide relief to free cash flow and financing requirements. With CBRE reporting just 1.4% vacancy across its primary North American markets and 80.4% of capacity under construction already preleased, additional barriers to entry should reinforce the scarcity value of operational assets. The relative beneficiaries should therefore be the businesses able to supply compute now, with a stronger claim on the economics of the investment cycle as physical expansion becomes harder. This should also create considerable scope for differentiation through stock selection, with the geographical distribution of development pipelines, particularly exposure to Texas and other jurisdictions facing tighter permitting restrictions, becoming an increasingly important determinant of execution risk, the timing of revenue realisation and ultimately relative valuations.

For risk assets in aggregate, we still see slower deployment and greater execution risk as an adverse development, notwithstanding the rotation towards sectors less exposed to the AI investment cycle. While the election removes an important source of political uncertainty, the argument for treating it as a clearing event seems less compelling when the outcome itself implies a more challenging investment environment for the AI build out, particularly given the extent of the swing was larger than expected. For rates, the combination of risk aversion, a potentially softer near-term investment impulse and possible modest financing deferrals should favour lower yields, although the geographical mobility of capital suggests caution in extrapolating this into a lasting collapse in either spending or issuance.

The scale and breadth of the demographic swing against Republicans suggest that Trump’s governing choices have weakened the coalition that returned him to office. The Iran war, tariffs and renewed pressure on household purchasing power appear to have undermined his affordability agenda, with the sharp rise in gasoline and diesel prices particularly damaging for rural and agricultural communities across the Midwest, where Republican losses have been pronounced. The overlap between higher fuel-price exposure and the swing against Republicans is striking, suggesting that the economic consequences of Trump’s policy choices have been felt particularly acutely in parts of his traditional electoral base.

Relative to the 2022 midterms, the Republican advantage among men has disappeared, having stood at 14 points, while its lead among white men has narrowed from 28 to 12 points. Even among white men without a college degree, arguably the most historically dependable constituency in the Republican electoral base, the margin has fallen from 46 to 30. The Republican advantage among non-college graduates more broadly has declined from 12 to four points, and among voters over 65 from 12 to three, while the Democratic margin among women has widened from eight to 18 points and among college graduates from ten to 26. These appear to be substantial reversals extending deep into the Republican base, consistent with voters responding to economic outcomes that may have fallen short of expectations. Alongside what looks like an erosion of Trump’s 2024 gains among younger and Hispanic voters, the results may leave Republicans weighing both the consequences of his policy choices and the potential fragility of a highly personalised coalition that may not persist without the President on the ballot in 2028.

We think that combination strengthens the case for a more conventional Republican nominee capable of recovering the political centre in 2028. Prediction markets have already begun repricing this shifting balance of power. For example, Ron DeSantis’s implied probability of securing the nomination has risen from roughly 4% before the results to around 19%, while JD Vance’s has fallen from approximately 36% to 31%, leaving him the favourite but with a diminished advantage. We are inclined to read the DeSantis move primarily as an increased premium on distance from the administration’s governing record. The Republican party could find itself carrying the liabilities of Trump’s time in office without the candidate-specific turnout advantages that helped assemble a broad but ultimately less stable coalition of voters.

We see two further important implications of the election for the strategic US macro outlook. First, the Democratic resurgence appears to have been considerably stronger among more centrist candidates than those on the party’s left flank. Across the 17 states that held Senate races in both 2024 and 2026, the average Democratic swing relative to the 2024 presidential election was 6.7 percentage points, but this fell to just 3.1 points among candidates endorsed by Bernie Sanders, compared with 8.1 points for those without his endorsement. While these comparisons may have been influenced by differences in state electorates and candidate characteristics, we think the divergence is striking given the scale of the national swing, suggesting that the electorate’s repudiation of the Trump administration should not necessarily be interpreted as an endorsement of a substantially more progressive economic agenda. The results may therefore strengthen the influence of the Democratic Party’s more moderate wing as attention turns towards 2028, with implications for the eventual direction of fiscal, tax and regulatory policy.

Furthermore, the election may have materially increased the political urgency of bringing the Iran war to a conclusion. Both President Trump and Vice President Vance have attributed Republican losses, at least in part, to the conflict, reinforcing the political costs of prolonging a war whose consequences for energy prices and household purchasing power have been particularly damaging among traditional Republican constituencies. We argued in Iran – Peak Gamma that Tehran’s strategic position resembled a long, high-strike oil call expiring around the US midterms, with its capacity to extract political concessions through disruption to energy markets approaching a maximum ahead of the election, before the time value of that leverage evaporated and escalation dominance was lost. Recent diplomatic developments in the immediate lead up to the midterms could be interpreted as a sign that Tehran may indeed be attempting to monetize its remaining leverage through a negotiated settlement. Notably, the election suggests that Washington’s incentives to reach an agreement may also have strengthened, which could bring the political calculus of both sides into closer alignment.

With substantial crude flows already being sustained through and around the Strait of Hormuz, we suspect a credible diplomatic resolution could precipitate further compression in energy risk premia and our analysis of the oil option market implies the market has begun to substantially reduce the upside premium embedded in the last week. Specifically, the three-month option-implied probability of Brent exceeding $120 has more than halved since 28th October, from 23% to 9%, while the one-month probability has collapsed from 27% to just 7%. Upside skew has also flattened across shorter maturities, suggesting that markets have been progressively removing the premium associated with a renewed escalation in the conflict. The direction and concentration of these distributional price adjustments are consistent with our thesis that the midterms could catalyse a resolution.

item.title: November: The Setup Improves
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: The election is over and markets are breathing a sigh of relief, with S&P 500 futures now 260bps and Nasdaq 100 futures 350bps off their overnight lows. This sets the stage for investors to rebuild equity exposure into year-end. October brought a significant reset across Technolo...
item.content:encoded:
The election is over and markets are breathing a sigh of relief, with S&P 500 futures now 260bps and Nasdaq 100 futures 350bps off their overnight lows.

This sets the stage for investors to rebuild equity exposure into year-end.

October brought a significant reset across Technology and the AI complex, but remarkably little broad-based selling. While the Nasdaq 100 declined nearly 10% over the past month, the equal-weight S&P 500 advanced nearly 5%, with investors rotating into other parts of the market rather than indiscriminately reducing equity exposure.

The underlying demand picture has also changed. Retail has bought US equities for 22 consecutive sessions, corporate buyback windows are reopening, and CTA positioning has fallen to -3.3 standard deviations, leaving considerable room for systematic buying as markets recover. Meanwhile, earnings continue to beat elevated expectations, while valuations across semiconductors and AI infrastructure have compressed sharply.

We believe the combination of light positioning, returning corporate demand, persistent retail buying, and historically favorable post-midterm seasonality creates a compelling setup for US equities into year-end. With the election behind us and volatility potentially normalizing, there is considerable capacity for investors to rebuild risk.

1. The Buyers are Coming Back

Retail: Twenty-Two Sessions of Buying into a Falling Tape.

Retail has been a net buyer of US cash equities on our platform for 22 consecutive sessions since October 5, accumulating nearly $33B in the sixth-longest and fifth-largest buying streak since 2017. Buying has averaged $1.5B per session, 1.4x the trailing-year average, as the S&P has fallen 2.0% over the same period. Of the 12 previous buying streaks lasting at least 15 sessions, the S&P advanced during 10, with a median gain of 2.2%. None occurred alongside a larger market decline.

Cash flow was concentrated in ETFs, but the single-name rotation favored semis and the AI build-out over recent winners and defensives. Year-to-date net equity buying has reached a record $251B, surpassing the previous full year high of $241B in 2021 and running 134% ahead of the same point last year.

Retail options activity has reflected a similar shift, with investors increasingly favoring index products and buying into weakness across Technology. October was the busiest October on record for our retail options platform, with index and ETF products accounting for nearly 60% of activity. Retail continued to buy dips in the broader market, trading 7% better to buy on S&P 500 down days while remaining roughly flat on up days.

Within more thematic activity, the rotation once again toward Semiconductors has been particularly pronounced. Activity ran 15% above its trailing-year average, with the sector accounting for nearly 40% of single-stock premium, roughly double its share a year ago.

Corporate Buybacks: The Blackout Window Reopens

Corporate repurchases are also set to return as Q3 earnings-related blackout windows expire. Less than a quarter of S&P 500 index weight was eligible to repurchase shares in mid-October, compared with approximately two-thirds by Election Day and an expected 85% by November 9. The reopening comes against a record year for buyback authorizations, with companies announcing $1.5T of new repurchase programs through November 2, already exceeding the previous full-year record set in 2025.

October alone saw $166B of new buyback authorizations, more than twice its historical average, with 30 programs of at least $1B announced since our October update. The recent pickup has also extended beyond Technology, broadening the potential base of corporate demand as repurchase windows reopen heading into year-end.

CTAs: From Long to -3.3σ

Our CTA model estimates aggregate US equity positioning at -3.3 standard deviations, in the sub-2nd percentile of its one-year range, in the 10th percentile of its history since 2018, and the lowest since March 31. Positioning has fallen from +1.7σ three months ago to -1.0σ one month ago, with CTAs now short for 26 consecutive sessions.

A sustained recovery through key technical levels could prompt trend-following strategies to rebuild equity exposure, adding another potential source of demand alongside retail accumulation and corporate repurchases.

2. Earnings Are Beating. Multiples Are Falling.

Corporate earnings have continued to exceed expectations despite entering Q3 reporting season against one of the highest bars in more than a decade. Consensus expectations called for 27% YoY S&P 500 EPS growth, with estimates having been revised higher heading into earnings. Through the first 304 reporters, representing 65% of index weight, 83% of companies have beaten EPS estimates, compared with a historical average of ~75%. This ranks among the ten strongest reporting seasons at a comparable stage since 2005.

Despite the strength in reported earnings, investors have been considerably less willing to reward companies for beating expectations. The index-weighted average earnings-day move has been −1.2%, the 2nd worst in 87 reporting seasons since 2005. The reaction has been particularly pronounced across Technology and Communication Services, where more than 90% of companies have beaten EPS estimates, yet only 35% and 18%, respectively, have traded higher following their reports.

The repricing has been most aggressive across the areas of the market experiencing the strongest earnings revisions. Since June 30, forward EPS estimates have risen 32% for Memory, 31% for AI Infrastructure, and 30% for Semiconductors. Over the same period, forward valuation multiples have contracted 50%, 36% and 35%, respectively. Nearly every company in these groups has seen earnings expectations improve, yet all 20 S&P 500 semiconductor constituents have experienced multiple compression. The trend has continued since our October update, with semiconductor estimates rising another 3% while valuations declined a further 7%.

The compression has been particularly pronounced in the Nasdaq 100, which now trades at 19.1x forward earnings, its lowest multiple since October 2022 and 24% below its January peak. Despite a 14% increase in forward earnings since June, the multiple has contracted 19%. Relative to the S&P 500, the Nasdaq now costs just a 5% premium, the smallest since January 2017 and well below its ten-year average of ~20%. Information Technology itself trades at 18.2x, its lowest multiple since March 2020.

Semiconductors have seen an even sharper reset. The S&P 500 semiconductors now trade at 13.8x forward earnings, 45% below the January peak and the lowest since July 2022.

Relative to the S&P 500, Semiconductors trade at a 25% discount, the widest since December 2018, having commanded a 66% premium at the height of the AI trade in June 2024. This is despite forward earnings estimates rising 30% since June, with the sector expected to account for nearly half of the S&P 500’s Q3 EPS growth despite representing less than one-fifth of index weight. With valuations having compressed substantially faster than earnings expectations, even a modest recovery in sentiment toward Technology (and Semiconductors in particular) could have a meaningful impact on the broader index.

3. Broadening Beneath the Surface

One of the more unusual features of the recent market weakness has been the extraordinary divergence between the largest index constituents and the broader market. Over the 20 sessions through November 2, the equal-weight S&P 500 gained more than 4% while the Nasdaq 100 declined nearly 10%, a 14% divergence ranking in the 99th percentile of all 20-session windows since 1990. The only wider rotations occurred during the dot-com era, while just four comparable episodes have taken place alongside a flat or declining market.

Despite a more than a 20% decline in semiconductor equities, most S&P 500 constituents have moved higher, with particularly strong performance across Staples, Utilities, Health Care, and Energy. Rather than the broad-based liquidation typically associated with a Technology drawdown of this magnitude, investors have largely rotated into other parts of the market.

Breadth has been equally remarkable: a median 53% of S&P 500 constituents advanced on the index’s down days over the period, compared with just 31% historically. The most extreme example came on October 29, when 406 of 503 constituents advanced despite SPY declining 38bps, the broadest positive breadth on a down day in our point-in-time history.

The reversal in leadership has also been usually quick. As recently as October 7, SPW vs. NDX had reached its lowest level since April 2000 before reversing sharply through the remainder of the month, now sitting in the 82nd percentile of its 1-year range. The RSI of SPW vs. NDX is now the most overbought it has been in more than 2 years, and a level only reached 20 times in the last two decades.

That distinction matters for the cap-weighted index. The ten largest S&P 500 companies still account for 37% of index weight, the Mag 7 for 33%, and NVDA alone for more than 235 of the smallest names in the index. The top ten’s share has fallen roughly 2.5 points since late September, but concentration remains historically high. In Q3, the ten largest names contributed 3.4 points of the S&P 500’s 2.3% gain, while the other constituents detracted 1.2 points. October was the reverse: broad participation was not enough to offset weakness in the largest stocks.

The same concentration can work in the other direction. With the average stock holding up and valuations across semiconductors and AI infrastructure substantially lower, renewed buying in the largest technology names would have an outsized effect on the benchmark. Passive index inflows would add to that demand, with 37 cents of every dollar allocated to the S&P 500 going to its ten largest constituents.

4. Positioning and the November Setup

The recent drawdown has been accompanied by a significant repricing in volatility, despite the absence of broad-based selling across US equities. One-month implied volatility is now elevated across nearly every major sector, with Energy, Communication Services, Consumer Staples, and Health Care all trading above the 95th percentile of their trailing-year ranges. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 are also trading at the 83rd and 96th percentiles, respectively, even as realized volatility in the broader market has remained relatively contained.

The VIX rose above 21 against S&P 500 one-month realized volatility below 11, alongside a meaningful steepening in index skew, with SPY one-month put/call skew now in the 73rd percentile of the past year. With implied volatility elevated relative to realized moves, a decline in volatility following the election and earnings season could allow volatility-targeting and other risk-managed strategies to rebuild equity exposure. This would add another potential source of demand alongside reopening corporate buyback windows and historically light systematic positioning.

The historical post-midterm setup is also particularly favorable. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has been higher six and twelve months after every midterm election, with a median twelve-month gain of 14.5%.

The fourth quarter of midterm years has historically been the strongest of the presidential cycle, with the S&P 500 averaging a 5.6% gain versus 2.9% across all years. November has been particularly strong, averaging +2.2% in midterm years, with the first half of the month positive nearly 80% of the time. The strength has been even more pronounced in Technology, with the Nasdaq 100 averaging nearly 5% in November and outperforming the S&P 500 in all post-midterm 12-month periods since 2002, by an average of roughly 10 percentage points.

This year’s market has entered the post-election period well behind its typical midterm-year seasonal path. The S&P 500 was lower from the end of September heading into the vote, compared with an average gain of approximately 3.5% by Election Day in previous midterm years. Historically, the fourth-quarter low has been established in October in 14 of 24 midterm years, followed by a median rally of nearly 10% into year-end.

GMI Bottom Line

The election is behind us, earnings remain strong, positioning has reset, and the calendar is turning more favorable. With uncertainty fading and several of the market’s largest buyers returning, we believe the path of least resistance for U.S. equities is higher into year-end.

item.title: Risks Abound
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: THIS IS WHAT A NARROW MARGIN OF SAFETY LOOKS LIKE. Last week I warned that a market increasingly dependent on the AI narrative had precious little room for disappointment. Capex itself has become a two-sided risk…spend too much and investors question the returns; pull back and th...
item.content:encoded:
THIS IS WHAT A NARROW MARGIN OF SAFETY LOOKS LIKE. Last week I warned that a market increasingly dependent on the AI narrative had precious little room for disappointment. Capex itself has become a two-sided risk…spend too much and investors question the returns; pull back and they question the demand. This week’s sharp technology sell-off has exposed that vulnerability…extraordinary growth is offering diminishing protection when delivering it consumes ever more cash. Free cash flow is becoming a dividing line, with investors penalising cash burn and deteriorating cash-generation prospects. For Alphabet, even a doubling of cloud revenues could not offset concerns about search monetisation and the financing demands of the buildout. In my mind, the market is becoming increasingly defensive…giving greater weight to threats to existing profit pools than the promise of future growth. In essence, the burden of proof is rising just as the financial commitments become harder to reverse. Anthropic’s S-1 illustrates the tension…H1 revenues surged to $16.3bn from $1.2bn a year earlier, with Q2 delivering $974mn of operating profit. Compute and infrastructure expenses fell from 251% of revenues in Q1 2025 to 48% in Q2 2026, as revenue growth outpaced the committed cost base and model efficiency improved. Yet the next buildout brings compute costs online ahead of the revenues they support…a mismatch Anthropic warns can squeeze margins even as the underlying economics improve. The competitive arithmetic remains demanding…as Frank Flight’s latest note highlights, consumption-weighted token prices have roughly halved over six months, token volumes have increased around fivefold and B200 rental rates have risen 27.5%. Cheaper intelligence is stimulating substantial usage, whilst scarce compute is becoming more expensive. Combining those price and rental changes implies a 2.55-fold increase in throughput merely to preserve the compute-related serving-margin percentage…an illustrative calculation, rather than an estimate of any individual lab’s profitability. The question is how much of each efficiency gain producers can retain before competition passes it through to customers. Locking in compute costs can reduce exposure to rising spot prices but creates an obligation to keep that capacity productively employed…the risk shifts towards future utilisation and pricing. Damodaran’s framework is useful for the same reason…it makes explicit how much the ANT investment case depends on premium positioning, durable margins and the reinvestment required to sustain growth.

 

Source: Ornn, Silicon Data, Citadel Securities, data as of Oct 2026. Figures are for illustrative purposes only. Past performance does not guarantee future returns

 

THE FED’S DECISION TO LEAVE RATES UNCHANGED AT 3.75–4%, with Cook and Hammack dissenting in favour of another 25bp hike suggests the direction of travel for policy rates remains intact as the Fed follows other central banks into what looks like an every-other-meeting cadence. Thursday’s data (Sep Core PCE +0.32%; Q3 GDP +3.4%; private domestic demand +4.9%) is a reminder that growth remains resilient and inflation is still elevated…a combination that provides little reason to declare the adjustment complete. Indeed, Chair Warsh remains “unwilling and unable” to call financial conditions tight, broadly welcoming tighter credit and more discerning capital allocation as an expected outcome of Fed action. That said, the Fed is clearly watching transmission through markets…this isn’t necessarily hawkish or dovish but implies that policy rate decisions are endogenous to broad FCI…so the more work the market does, the less the Fed needs to do and vice versa. There were also changes to the schedule: it looks like the October meeting will become a strategy meeting with no statement or policy decision, implying Warsh is making some incremental changes to the Fed’s modus operandi. I don’t read this as particularly relevant for the policy direction and expect another 25bp hike in December, provided growth remains resilient and financial conditions avoid a disruptive tightening. Ultimately, with nominal GDP growth still close to 6%, returning inflation sustainably to target requires tighter financial conditions. The question for markets is how much further FCI must tighten before the Fed considers them restrictive enough. In the long term, productivity is the critical release valve…allowing more growth with less inflationary pressure, whilst expanding the tax base and improving the longer-term fiscal arithmetic. This is why the AI boom matters well beyond technology stocks…its investment impulse is already supporting demand, whilst the scale and timing of a sustained AI-led acceleration in aggregate productivity remain uncertain. The mismatch in timing of the macroeconomic costs (inflation) versus the payoff (productivity) is likely to keep policy tight until we see clearer evidence of productivity in the economic data…which history tells us takes time. 

 

 

THE BULLISH NARRATIVE IS STRUGGLING TO ABSORB AN INCREASING NUMBER OF RISKS. A Democratic sweep of Congress seems increasingly plausible, with the latest Ipsos survey showing a nine-point advantage among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot, whilst prediction markets put the chances above 90% for the House and 70% for the Senate. I would be wary of assuming that divided government automatically delivers fiscal restraint or a quieter policy environment…it could equally make a durable fiscal settlement harder to achieve. Meanwhile, Israel’s deadlocked election keeps Netanyahu in office during coalition negotiations, with pressure for further action against Iran likely to persist. Reports point to preparations for a possible multi-day US campaign after the mid-terms, pending President Trump’s final decision. A 3-to-10-day exchange largely contained to military targets is one scenario…but it requires both sides to keep accepting the other’s definition of a proportionate response. Israeli strikes or assassinations could induce Iranian attacks on energy infrastructure, turning a supposedly limited operation into a much more consequential economic shock. Ukraine’s reported strike on a Russian refinery also ends a two-week pause in attacks…another reminder of how fragile restraint around energy infrastructure remains. Moreover, the Binance hack adds to investor anxiety around cyber risk, coming just a week after warnings that AI is accelerating the exploitation of software vulnerabilities. AI involvement in this particular attack remains unconfirmed, but the incident arrives as concerns about AI-enabled threats to the financial system are growing. This is where the risks begin to reinforce one another. Renewed disruption to oil supply could weaken real incomes and sustain inflation, complicating the Fed’s reaction function further just as the AI complex needs ever greater access to capital. Within AI, falling token prices and rising compute costs increase the importance of maintaining inference-efficiency gains; a slowdown in those gains would make the margin assumptions much harder to defend. Remember, technological progress can coexist with disappointing investment returns. In sum, the strength of the AI narrative has so far overshadowed mounting political, geopolitical, and financial risks…but as these proliferate, any loss of confidence in AI returns leaves the economy and markets with very little margin for error.

item.title: Tokenomics 2.0
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Consumption weighted token prices have declined approximately 50% over six months and average token prices have declined 62% at the frontier, reflecting both the growing share of cheaper open-weight models and price cuts by proprietary providers, likely driven by some combination...
item.content:encoded:
Consumption weighted token prices have declined approximately 50% over six months and average token prices have declined 62% at the frontier, reflecting both the growing share of cheaper open-weight models and price cuts by proprietary providers, likely driven by some combination of improved inference efficiency and competitive pressure. Increased competition from open-weight models may exert pressure on margins at the frontier through time, but the expansion of token volume suggests overall inference demand is accelerating.

Open-weight models now account for around 65-70% of smart routing token volume, potentially putting pressure on excess rents at the frontier as cheaper models become “good enough” for a growing range of enterprise tasks, especially given US-developed open-weight models offer greater flexibility around customisation, hosting and data control. Caution is warranted in extrapolating from OpenRouter and Vercel data, since users who self-select into model-routing platforms may be more willing to experiment with and switch between models, exhibiting less inertia than the broader AI customer base; however the direction of travel is nevertheless informative, especially as we expect adoption to become increasingly cost-conscious through time.

The recent stall in total expenditure in Ramp’s monthly spend data provides some further grounds for caution, as it shows essentially no growth in overall enterprise spend in the last two months (Aug and Sept), likely reflecting the interaction of lower token prices with increased volume. The data also implies that 80% of spend on frontier labs is driven by 1% of firms, and that the top 1% spent $9,568 per employee per month in Sept vs the median firm that spent $15.7 per employee per month, illustrating how concentrated spending remains. The recent plateau may prove important as total expenditure determines the revenues available to remunerate the AI investment cycle, and it appears that some combination of lower prices and increased competition from open-source may be causing total spend to flatline. The upcoming October release will be important as more timely token volume data from October imply a further acceleration of inference demand, but the implications for total spend remain unclear given shifts in token prices and composition of spend.

Token volumes have risen approximately 5x over the last 6 months and around 50% over the last four weeks, consistent with a substantial demand response as intelligence becomes cheaper. Where that expansion exceeds improvements in computational efficiency, demand for GPU-hours increases, and GPU rental rates suggest that available compute capacity remains scarce: H100 rentals are up approximately 14% over six months and 7% over the last 30 days, while B200 rentals have risen 27.5% over six months, implying robust demand for compute. Continued strength in older H100s is particularly striking against the depreciation one would ordinarily expect from technological obsolescence, implying sellers of scarce compute are well placed to extract rents.

A firm’s margin on each additional unit of output is the difference between its selling price and marginal cost, so falling output prices and rising input costs squeeze margins unless productivity improves sufficiently to compensate. For the frontier labs, competition from cheaper open-weight models can exert both pressures simultaneously, pushing token prices lower whilst stimulating inference demand that bids up the cost of compute. At unchanged inference efficiency, higher GPU rental rates increase the marginal cost of supplying a token, leaving the frontier receiving less for what it sells whilst paying more to produce it. The question is therefore whether improvements in tokens served per GPU-hour (inference efficiency) can offset both the decline in selling prices and the increase in compute costs in perpetuity. Gross margin can be approximated as follows, assuming compute dominates serving costs and holding workload mix constant:

Using the 27.5% rise in B200 GPU rental rates as an illustrative increase in compute costs, combined with the 50% decline in average token prices requires throughput to increase 2.55-fold, merely to preserve the gross-margin. This is not an unsurmountable issue, as reporting suggests that inference efficiency gains in the last year have been substantial, and compute costs can be locked in via multi year deals. However the marginal economics of inference can still remain a source of pressure, particularly on a forward basis, should open source competition intensify, or should progress on inference efficiency stall. These calculations are illustrative only and intended to highlight the efficiency requirement rather than estimate any individual lab’s margins, since public rental benchmarks differ from contracted compute costs and published token prices differ from realised revenues.

Hence, a clear focus is whether inference efficiency gains can continue to support margins despite intense competition for both market share and compute, particularly as the easier improvements or low-hanging fruit may, through time, become exhausted. New hardware offers greater throughput but also commands higher prices, absorbing some of the incremental benefit. Moreover, as efficiency improves, those same benefits may apply to open-weight models too, such that another round of price cuts may stimulate further inference and renew the pressure on scarce compute, leaving the frontier obliged to deliver further successive gains simply to defend its existing margins. None of this implies that the fundamentals of the business model are broken; however, markets move on gaps between expectations and reality, and we question whether expectations for frontier profitability fully accommodate sustained competition that passes efficiency gains through to customers whilst infrastructure suppliers capture the benefits of scarcity in the form of excess rents.

We consequently see a more nuanced outlook for the AI ecosystem, with strong inference demand favouring suppliers of scarce compute as competition raises questions around excess returns at the frontier. The economics may resemble those of airlines and airports, with frontier labs as the established airlines, providing an essential service to the economy in a highly competitive market and sees open-weight models as the low-cost carriers, expanding the market through cheaper fares whilst constraining what incumbents can charge. The hyperscalers’ infrastructure businesses resemble the airports, with stickier demand and greater scope for higher, more durable margins from supplying scarce compute, and a commercial architecture that is model agnostic in the long run. A reassessment of profitability at the frontier on margin or commoditisation concerns would nevertheless be challenging for the complex as a whole, given how much infrastructure investment rests on future spending commitments. Within that framing, we see the hyperscalers as potentially the most durable beneficiaries of growing inference demand, with diversified cash flows and strong balance sheets allowing them to fund additional capacity and withstand a reassessment of frontier profitability more comfortably than leveraged neoclouds.

Jim Esposito, President of Citadel Securities, opened the Future of Global Markets Conference with remarks on the convergence of technological innovation and geopolitical change. He highlighted the accelerating impact of AI, the growing intersection of technology and national power and the critical role of capital markets in financing the next era of economic transformation.

Key Takeaways

  • Technology and Geopolitics: Rapid technological advancement and geopolitical shifts are reshaping the global order, with computing power, energy and capital increasingly becoming instruments of national power.
  • AI Beyond the Digital World: AI is moving into factories, laboratories, transportation, energy systems and defense, expanding the boundaries of innovation.
  • Capital Fuels Innovation: Like the Industrial Revolution, today’s technological transformation has the potential to create entirely new industries, with capital markets playing a critical role in financing their development.
  • Citadel Securities at Scale: With 1,800+ professionals globally, Citadel Securities executes roughly a quarter of U.S. equity trading volume and processes nearly $800 billion in daily notional trading volume, leveraging its scale to deliver deeper liquidity, sharper pricing and market insights.

item.title: A Conversation with Ken Griffin
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Citadel Securities founder Ken Griffin spoke with Bloomberg’s Dani Burger at our recent Future of Global Markets Conference. Ken and Dani discussed the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, and how investors are becoming more discerning in this rapidly growing mark...
item.content:encoded:
Citadel Securities founder Ken Griffin spoke with Bloomberg’s Dani Burger at our recent Future of Global Markets Conference. Ken and Dani discussed the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, and how investors are becoming more discerning in this rapidly growing market. Read the key takeaways below.

1. Artificial Intelligence: Transformative Potential and the Future of Work

  • The advancement in AI models over just the past year has been absolutely tremendous. In a number of fields, AI is literally game-changing. Work that used to take our PhDs and master’s-level employees four to six weeks can now be completed in a matter of hours.
  • There are three implications:

    –  For workers: AI poses a real threat to certain white-collar jobs. We need to embrace reskilling in a profound way. There’s plenty of talk about it, but very little action.

    –  For corporate America: Competitive moats are being filled in by bulldozers. Companies will need to innovate faster, create more customer value and take costs out faster. That’s ultimately a win for the American consumer.

    –  For entrepreneurs: This is a golden era for new business formation. Startups will unleash products we’ve never even thought of and create opportunities for people who don’t have perfect pedigrees to build successful careers.

  • The history of our free market is that we go through transitions like this. They’re challenging for incumbents and difficult for workers, but ultimately our lives are better.

2. AI Markets: Investors Are Becoming More Discerning

  • For the last several years, investors have largely bought into the AI theme: We’re going to spend hundreds of billions or trillions on data centers and compute. Buy the hyperscalers, buy the chip companies, buy the entire supply chain.
  • Now we’re reaching a point where people are becoming more discerning. Who actually earns the economic rents? Where are the real supply constraints? How long will today’s extraordinary margins persist?
  • GPU overcapacity is a significant risk. GPUs have very low marginal operating costs, much like airlines. When capacity exceeds demand, pricing can go into freefall. We saw a similar dynamic during the telecom buildout in 2000, when excess fiber capacity drove telecommunications prices sharply lower.
  • Investors are also reconsidering the useful life of GPUs. Five- or six-year-old chips may command extraordinary pricing today, but that doesn’t mean those economics will persist for another five or six years. Revenue and valuation assumptions for years seven, eight and nine need to be reconsidered.
  • Corporate America is becoming much more sophisticated about extracting value from AI. Companies are asking where they truly need expensive, state-of-the-art models from OpenAI and Anthropic, and where open-source models can do the job at a fraction of the cost.
  • There is a tension between the enormous spending ambitions of foundational model companies and their customers’ efforts to maximize returns and control costs. The question is whether these models become so indispensable—potentially by solving problems like curing cancer—that customers will pay almost any price.

3. Is AI a Bubble?

  • There are almost certainly bubbles within this moment in time. Radical transformations of our economy are generally intertwined with bubbles.
  • Think about the internet in 1999 and 2000. Some companies had pretty fanciful business models, but the internet fundamentally transformed our lives. I just wish I’d kept my Amazon stock.
  • We’ve seen this with other transformative technologies, including the railroads. What’s left in the wake of these bubbles is often game-changing for the world, and the companies that emerge on the other side can be market leaders for decades.

item.title: Europe’s Choice: Competitiveness, Security, and the Future of the European Union
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Mario Draghi, former Prime Minister of Italy and former President of the European Central Bank, joined Bloomberg Television’s Lisa Abramowicz for a discussion on Europe’s economic outlook, competitiveness and geopolitical challenges. The conversation explored fiscal pressures, mo...
item.content:encoded:
Mario Draghi, former Prime Minister of Italy and former President of the European Central Bank, joined Bloomberg Television’s Lisa Abramowicz for a discussion on Europe’s economic outlook, competitiveness and geopolitical challenges. The conversation explored fiscal pressures, monetary policy, AI adoption, energy security and the reforms needed to strengthen Europe’s position in the global economy.

Key Takeaways

  • Growth and Fiscal Stability: Europe’s sluggish growth and rising fiscal pressures are testing economic stability, with Draghi emphasizing inflation control as the European Central Bank’s priority and a high threshold for intervention in sovereign bond markets.
  • European Competitiveness: Fragmented regulations and incomplete integration of services and capital markets are limiting companies’ ability to scale, underscoring the need for structural reforms to unlock investment and growth.
  • AI and Innovation: Europe’s strongest opportunity lies in accelerating AI adoption across industries such as advanced manufacturing, healthcare and finance, rather than competing directly with the U.S. and China in building computing infrastructure.
  • Energy Independence: Expanding renewables, modernizing electricity grids and mobilizing private capital are essential to reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels and supporting Europe’s transition to a more electrified economy.
  • Security and European Unity: Changing transatlantic relations are pushing Europe to assume greater responsibility for its defense, while Draghi expressed confidence that shared interests will preserve European unity despite political uncertainty.

item.title: Fireside Conversation with Eric Glyman, CEO of Ramp
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Eric Glyman, Co-founder and CEO of Ramp, joined Frank Flight, Head of Macro Strategy at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on how AI is reshaping business operations, productivity and economic growth. Drawing on Ramp’s corporate spending data, Glyman explored the pace of AI ado...
item.content:encoded:
Eric Glyman, Co-founder and CEO of Ramp, joined Frank Flight, Head of Macro Strategy at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on how AI is reshaping business operations, productivity and economic growth. Drawing on Ramp’s corporate spending data, Glyman explored the pace of AI adoption, its implications for the workforce and the evolving economics of artificial intelligence.

Key Takeaways

  • Uneven AI Adoption: While a majority of Ramp’s customers now spend on AI, adoption remains highly concentrated, with the top 1% of businesses accounting for approximately 80% of AI spending.
  • Evolving AI Economics: Declining model costs and intensifying competition are reshaping the AI landscape, potentially shifting value toward application-layer companies that translate intelligence into business outcomes.
  • AI and Business Growth: Ramp’s research found that businesses with higher AI adoption experienced stronger revenue growth, with high-intensity adopters increasing headcount approximately 12% faster than before adoption.
  • Organizational Transformation: AI is prompting companies to rethink traditional workflows and organizational structures, integrating intelligent systems into core functions rather than simply automating individual tasks.
  • Managing AI Investment: As spending on AI becomes a significant corporate expense, businesses will increasingly need tools to manage costs, evaluate returns and optimize their use of AI.

item.dc:creator: ovaughn

He highlighted the firm’s technology infrastructure, data-driven an...
item.content:encoded:
Jeff Maurone, Technology COO at Citadel Securities, shared how the firm leverages AI, quantitative research and proprietary technology to deliver actionable market insights and high-quality execution for clients. He highlighted the firm’s technology infrastructure, data-driven analytics and growing collaboration with clients to anticipate market dynamics and solve complex trading challenges.

Key Takeaways

  • AI-Driven Insights: AI and autonomous agents are amplifying human intuition, enabling Citadel Securities to systematically analyze vast amounts of data and answer client questions before they are asked.
  • Predictive Market Analytics: Proprietary tools such as Breakout Probability and Positioning NowCast combine market flows, positioning data and historical trends to provide earlier visibility into shifts in investor holdings.
  • Real-Time Credit Intelligence: The firm’s investment-grade credit heat map provides a customized, real-time view of corporate bond spreads, helping clients track market movements across issuers and sectors.
  • Technology at Scale: Citadel Securities’ research infrastructure supports more than 500 quantitative researchers and over 200 petabytes of data, with 65% of colleagues writing code to develop proprietary trading technology.
  • Client Collaboration: The firm has engaged with more than 100 client technology teams to explore AI adoption, agent development and quantitative research, strengthening partnerships and developing solutions to address client needs.
